module_title: Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code (IBC), 2016: Foundational Principles
introduction: This foundational level introduces the Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code, 2016 (IBC). It explains the historic legislative shift from a 'Debtor-in-Possession' to a 'Creditor-in-Control' regime, outlines the institutional infrastructure of bankruptcy, and introduces the default thresholds required to trigger the resolution process.

core_concepts.title: Why the IBC was Enacted
core_concepts.description: Prior to 2016, India's insolvency framework was fragmented across multiple overlapping laws (SICA, SARFAESI, CDR, RDDBFI). It took an average of 4.3 years to resolve a default, severely trapping bank capital. The IBC consolidated these laws into a single, time-bound code to maximize the value of assets, promote entrepreneurship, and balance the interests of all stakeholders.

core_concepts.title: The Paradigm Shift: Creditor-in-Control
core_concepts.description: Under older laws like SICA, management stayed with the debtor while sick companies were revived, allowing promoters to siphon off funds while enjoying protection from creditors ('Debtor-in-Possession'). The IBC reversed this: the moment a default occurs, management is stripped from the promoters and handed over to an independent professional controlled by the creditors ('Creditor-in-Control').

core_concepts.title: The Four Pillars of IBC Infrastructure
core_concepts.description:
The IBC functions via a unique four-pronged institutional ecosystem:
1. Insolvency and Bankruptcy Board of India (IBBI): The apex statutory regulator.
2. Insolvency Professionals (IPs) & Agencies (IPAs): Licensed professionals who take active management of the debtor company.
3. Information Utilities (IUs): Centralized digital databases that store authenticated credit information to prove defaults instantly.
4. Adjudicating Authority (AA): The National Company Law Tribunal (NCLT) for corporates, and Debt Recovery Tribunal (DRT) for individuals.

core_concepts.title: The ₹1 Crore Threshold
core_concepts.description: To protect Micro, Small, and Medium Enterprises (MSMEs) from frivolous bankruptcy filings, the minimum threshold of default required to trigger the Corporate Insolvency Resolution Process (CIRP) against a corporate debtor was permanently raised to **₹1 Crore** (up from the original statutory minimum of ₹1 Lakh).

important_entities.name: Corporate Debtor vs. Creditor
important_entities.key_fact: The debtor is the company that owes the money; the creditor is the one who lent it.
important_entities.significance: Under Section 3(8), a Corporate Debtor is a corporate person who owes a debt to any person. Creditors are fundamentally divided into two distinct legal classes: Financial Creditors (banks/lenders) and Operational Creditors (suppliers, employees, contractors).

trap_alerts_and_exceptions.alert_title: The 'IBC is a Recovery Tool' Trap
trap_alerts_and_exceptions.explanation: Examiners heavily test this conceptual boundary. The Supreme Court has repeatedly ruled (e.g., *Swiss Ribbons v. Union of India*) that the IBC is **NOT a debt recovery mechanism**. It is a beneficial legislation meant for the *reorganization and insolvency resolution* of corporate debtors. Recovery is a coercive process, whereas resolution is an economic revival process.

mnemonics_and_tricks.memory_phrase: B I P A (Board, Information Utility, Professionals, Adjudicating Authority)
mnemonics_and_tricks.explanation: Remember BIPA to quickly map out the entire statutory ecosystem enabling the operation of the Code.

exam_strategy_tips: If an exam question asks 'Who acts as the Adjudicating Authority for a corporate person under the IBC?', always choose the **National Company Law Tribunal (NCLT)**, not the civil court or High Court.
